course.title: UX/UI Design Fundamentals
course.description: A hands-on first course in user experience and interface design — from the design process and user research to wireframes, prototypes, and usability testing. Topic scope follows Google Career Certificates (UX Design), targeting the same UX-certificate-style foundations, with all prose original.

questions.prompt: UX (user experience) design is best described as designing…
options: only the colors and fonts of a screen
the whole experience of using a product, so it is useful and easy
questions.explanation: UX covers the end-to-end experience; visual styling (UI) is one part of it.

questions.prompt: The five phases of the design-thinking process are…
questions.explanation: Empathize → define → ideate → prototype → test, iterating as you go.

questions.prompt: A persona is…
options: a real named customer you must contact
a fictional but research-based profile of a target user
questions.explanation: Personas summarize real research into a representative user profile.

questions.prompt: Information architecture is mainly about…
options: how content is organized, labeled, and navigated
questions.explanation: IA is the structure and labeling that helps people find things.

questions.prompt: A wireframe is…
options: a low-detail layout showing structure and priority
questions.explanation: Wireframes focus on layout and hierarchy, not visual polish.

questions.prompt: Usability testing means…
options: asking users if they like the colors
watching real users attempt tasks to find problems
questions.explanation: You observe people doing tasks and note where they struggle.

questions.prompt: Which is an accessibility best practice?
options: sufficient text-to-background contrast and alt text for images
tiny tap targets to save space
questions.explanation: Contrast, alt text, and keyboard access make products usable by more people.

questions.prompt: The main reason to prototype before building is to…
options: test ideas cheaply and catch problems early
questions.explanation: Prototypes let you learn and iterate before costly development.

lessons.title: What UX is and the design process
lessons.grammar_note: Remember the five phases in order: empathize → define → ideate → prototype → test.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what UX design is and walk through the five phases of the design process. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which phase comes right after 'define'?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: User experience (UX) design is the practice of making a product useful, usable, and enjoyable for the people who use it. The *user interface* (UI) — the buttons, type, and color you touch — is one visible layer of UX. Most teams work through a *design-thinking* cycle: *empathize* (understand real users), *define* (state the problem clearly), *ideate* (generate many possible solutions), *prototype* (build a rough version), and *test* (put it in front of users). It is not a straight line: findings in the test phase often send you back to redefine the problem.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Imagine a food-delivery app whose checkout screen shows a single long form of 14 fields with no headings. Critiquing it against the process: the team skipped *empathize* (they never watched hungry users on phones) and *define* (the real problem — 'people abandon a slow checkout' — was never stated). An improved version groups fields into 'Address', 'Payment', and 'Confirm', shows a 3-step progress bar, and defaults to the saved address. That redesign came from re-running empathize and define, not from adding graphics.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each activity to a phase: (1) interviewing five users about their commute, (2) writing 'users need a faster way to top up their transit card', (3) sketching six different top-up screens, (4) building a clickable mockup, (5) watching a user try to top up and timing them. Answers: 1-empathize, 2-define, 3-ideate, 4-prototype, 5-test.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating UX as 'just how it looks' — usefulness and flow matter more than polish. Mistake: assuming the process runs once, top to bottom, instead of looping. Exit: (a) Which phase turns messy research into a clear problem statement? (b) Name the phase where you first put something in front of a real user. Answers: define; test (a prototype is tested, so 'test').

lessons.title: User research and personas
lessons.grammar_note: Qualitative research tells you 'why'; quantitative tells you 'how many'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose a basic research method and turn findings into a persona. Warm-up: is a one-hour interview qualitative or quantitative?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *User research* replaces guessing with evidence about who your users are and what they need. *Qualitative* methods (interviews, contextual observation) reveal motivations and pain points — the 'why'. *Quantitative* methods (surveys, analytics) count behavior — the 'how many'. You then synthesize findings into a *persona*: a fictional, research-based profile with a name, goals, frustrations, and context, so the whole team designs for a concrete person instead of a vague 'user'. A *user need statement* — '[persona] needs [need] in order to [goal]' — keeps research actionable.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A team interviews eight caregivers using a pharmacy app. Reviewing a draft persona, they had written 'Busy Person, 25-65, likes convenience' — too broad to design for. Improved, the persona reads: 'Marisol, 38, cares for an aging parent, checks refills late at night on her phone, frustrated when she can't tell which prescription is due.' That specificity points straight at a design fix: a clear 'due soon' status on each medication.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as qualitative or quantitative: (1) a 500-person survey on feature use, (2) sitting beside a user as they book a trip, (3) analytics showing 40% drop-off at step 3, (4) an open-ended 'walk me through your morning' interview. Then: (5) write a one-line user need statement for Marisol above. Answers: 1-quantitative, 2-qualitative, 3-quantitative, 4-qualitative, 5-e.g. 'Marisol needs an at-a-glance refill status in order to avoid missing her parent's medication.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: designing a persona from your own assumptions instead of data — that is a 'proto-persona' at best and should be validated. Mistake: leading interview questions ('Don't you love this feature?'). Exit: (a) Which method best explains *why* users abandon a flow? (b) What three parts belong in a user need statement? Answers: a qualitative method like interviews or observation; persona + need + goal.

lessons.title: Information architecture and user flows
lessons.grammar_note: IA = how content is organized; a user flow = the path a user takes to reach a goal.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Organize content into a sensible structure and map a user flow. Warm-up: what do you call the menu structure that helps people find content?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Information architecture* (IA) is how you organize, label, and connect content so people can find what they need. Good IA uses categories and labels that match users' mental models, which you can check with a *card sort* (users group and name items themselves). A *user flow* is the step-by-step path a person takes to complete a goal — for example, sign-up → verify email → set preferences → home. *Sitemaps* show the overall structure; *flows* show movement through it. Clear IA reduces the number of steps and dead ends between a user and their goal.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Critique a settings screen that lists 'Notifications', 'Privacy', 'Sounds', 'Blocked users', and 'Data & storage' in random order with no groups. Users hunt for 'Blocked users' under three wrong labels first. Improved IA groups them: 'Account & privacy' (Privacy, Blocked users, Data), 'Alerts' (Notifications, Sounds). A card sort with six users confirmed people expected 'Blocked users' to live under privacy, not a top-level item. The flow to block someone drops from five taps to three.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For a library app, group these into 2-3 labeled categories: Search, My loans, Renew, Fines, Reading history, Account settings, Help. Then (write the flow) list the steps a user takes to renew a book. Answers (one good grouping): 'My library' (My loans, Renew, Reading history), 'Account' (Fines, Account settings), 'Support' (Search, Help). Renew flow: open My loans → select the book → tap Renew → confirm new due date.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: organizing content the way the company is structured instead of the way users think. Mistake: confusing a sitemap (structure) with a user flow (movement toward a goal). Exit: (a) Which research method validates your category labels with real users? (b) Sitemap or flow: which shows the path to complete a task? Answers: card sort; user flow.

questions.prompt: Which phase turns research into a clear problem statement?
questions.explanation: Define frames the problem before you generate solutions.

questions.prompt: An interview that reveals *why* users behave a certain way is…
questions.explanation: Qualitative methods explain motivations and reasons.

questions.prompt: A good persona is…
questions.explanation: Specific, research-based personas guide design decisions.

questions.prompt: A card sort is used to…
questions.explanation: Users group and name items, revealing their mental model.

questions.prompt: A user flow shows…
options: the step-by-step path to complete a goal
questions.explanation: Flows map movement toward a goal.

questions.prompt: A user need statement follows the pattern…
questions.explanation: '[Persona] needs [need] in order to [goal].'

lessons.title: Wireframing and prototyping
lessons.grammar_note: Fidelity = how finished it looks. Low-fi = rough; high-fi = polished.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sketch a wireframe and explain when to raise fidelity. Warm-up: should a first wireframe use real brand colors?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *wireframe* is a low-detail layout that shows structure, content priority, and where elements go — usually grayscale boxes and placeholder text. It answers 'what goes where and what matters most', not 'what color is it'. A *prototype* makes a design interactive so users can click through it. *Fidelity* describes how finished something looks: *low-fidelity* (paper sketches, gray boxes) is fast and invites honest feedback; *high-fidelity* (real colors, content, and clickable flows) is closer to the final product and better for detailed usability tests. Start low, learn, then raise fidelity.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Critique a wireframe for a news app home screen that gives equal size to the logo, a newsletter ad, and the top story. Visual priority is wrong: the reader came for stories. Improved, the wireframe makes the lead story a large block at the top, demotes the ad to a slim strip, and uses a clear heading hierarchy (H1 headline, smaller sub-links). Because it is low-fidelity, the team happily tore it up and redrew it three times in an hour — something they'd resist doing to a polished screen.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Decide low- or high-fidelity for each situation: (1) first ten minutes brainstorming layouts, (2) testing whether users notice a new checkout button's exact color and label, (3) getting quick reactions to three different screen structures, (4) a final stakeholder sign-off demo. Then (5) name one thing a wireframe should NOT include yet. Answers: 1-low, 2-high, 3-low, 4-high, 5-final colors/branding (or real imagery).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: polishing pixels before the structure is right — high fidelity too early wastes effort and makes people afraid to change it. Mistake: thinking a wireframe and a prototype are the same; a prototype is interactive. Exit: (a) Which fidelity invites the most honest, fast feedback? (b) What does a wireframe prioritize over color? Answers: low-fidelity; structure and content hierarchy.

lessons.title: Usability testing and accessibility
lessons.grammar_note: Test tasks, not opinions: ask users to *do* something, then watch.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Plan a small usability test and apply core accessibility checks. Warm-up: is 'Do you like this screen?' a good usability-test task?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Usability testing* means giving real users realistic *tasks* and observing where they hesitate, err, or give up — you watch behavior rather than collect opinions. Even five users typically surface most major problems. Write neutral tasks ('add a coat to your cart and check out'), stay quiet while they work, and note *severity*. *Accessibility* ensures people with disabilities can use the product: provide *alt text* for images, ensure sufficient color *contrast*, never rely on color alone to convey meaning, support full *keyboard navigation*, use large enough tap targets, and label form fields for screen readers. Accessible design usually improves usability for everyone.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Critique a signup form tested with five users: three fail because the only error signal is red text with no message ('color alone'), and a screen-reader user can't tell which field is wrong because inputs have no labels. Improved: each error shows an icon plus a written message ('Enter a valid email'), fields have visible labels tied to inputs, and the submit button is reachable by keyboard with a visible focus ring. A re-test drops the failure rate to zero — the fixes were accessibility fixes that helped every user.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Rewrite these into good usability tasks or flag the accessibility issue: (1) 'What do you think of the menu?' (2) a button that says 'Click the green one' (3) an image of a chart with no description (4) 'Do you find this easy?' (5) fields with placeholder-only labels that vanish on typing. Answers: (1) 'Find and open your order history.' (2) also give a text label, not color alone. (3) add alt text describing the chart's point. (4) 'Add two items and remove one.' (5) use persistent visible labels.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: asking for opinions instead of watching tasks — people are polite and unreliable narrators. Mistake: treating accessibility as an add-on at the end instead of a design requirement. Exit: (a) About how many users reveal most major usability problems? (b) Name two accessibility checks beyond color contrast. Answers: about five; alt text, keyboard navigation, field labels, adequate tap-target size (any two).

items.translation: a fictional, research-based profile representing a target user
items.example: The team designed the refill screen for Marisol, their primary persona.

items.translation: a low-detail layout showing structure and content priority, not final visuals
items.example: She sketched a grayscale wireframe before choosing any colors.

items.translation: an interactive draft of a design that users can click through to test
items.example: They tested a clickable prototype before writing any code.

items.translation: how content is organized, labeled, and connected so people can find it
items.example: Good information architecture cut the settings flow from five taps to three.

items.translation: a visual cue that signals how an element can be used
items.example: A raised, shadowed button has a clear affordance that it is tappable.

items.translation: designing so people with disabilities can perceive and use the product
items.example: Accessibility checks include alt text, contrast, and keyboard navigation.

questions.prompt: A wireframe mainly communicates…
questions.explanation: Wireframes prioritize layout and priority over visual polish.

questions.prompt: The best usability-test prompt is…
questions.explanation: Give users a realistic task and watch what they do.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many users reveal most major usability issues?
questions.explanation: About five users surface the majority of serious problems.

questions.prompt: Which is an accessibility requirement?
questions.explanation: Never rely on color alone; provide alt text, contrast, and labels.

questions.prompt: Starting low-fidelity is useful because it…
options: is fast and invites honest change
questions.explanation: Low-fi is cheap to change, so feedback is more honest.

questions.prompt: An affordance is…
options: a visual cue for how to use an element
questions.explanation: Affordances signal possible actions, like a button that looks pressable.

lessons.title: Applied project: design an app screen end-to-end

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one everyday task (e.g. topping up a transit card, booking a haircut, splitting a bill). Design a single app screen for it end-to-end, on paper or in any tool. You will plan, not ship — the goal is to move through the process deliberately.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Research: write one user need statement in the form '[persona] needs [need] in order to [goal]', based on at least two quick questions you'd ask a real user. 2) Flow: list the 3-5 steps a user takes to finish the task. 3) Wireframe: sketch the screen as grayscale boxes, marking the single most important element. 4) Usability plan: write two neutral test tasks you'd give a user and name one thing you'd measure (e.g. time, errors). 5) Accessibility: list two checks you applied (contrast, alt text, labels, keyboard, tap size).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The need statement names a specific persona, need, and goal. ✔ The flow has clear, ordered steps with no dead ends. ✔ The wireframe shows hierarchy (one element clearly dominant) and uses no final colors. ✔ Test tasks ask the user to *do* something, not to give an opinion. ✔ At least two concrete accessibility checks are listed. If all five are true, you've run a real, if small, UX design process.
